paragraphs.text: Sophia and Oliver were very excited when Miss Parker brought a glass terrarium into the classroom. Inside, on a fresh twig, was a bright jade-green chrysalis decorated with tiny golden dots. Miss Parker told the class that this was a monarch butterfly in its pupa stage. The students took turns recording its size and color in their science journals every morning.

For seven days, the chrysalis remained completely still. But on the eighth morning, Sophia noticed that the outer shell had turned transparent. Through the thin shell, the dark pattern of folded orange and black wings was clearly visible. Oliver called Miss Parker immediately because they knew the butterfly was ready to hatch.

Suddenly, the bottom of the chrysalis split open. The butterfly pushed itself out and hung upside down from the empty shell. Its body looked thick, and its wet wings were crumpled. Over the next hour, the butterfly pumped fluid into its wings until they became large, smooth, and dry. That afternoon, the children carried the cage out to the flower garden and cheered as the butterfly took flight.
